source.title: Differentiable learning of matricized DNFs and its application to Boolean networks

record.tranche_reason: Tests generalization after learning error reaches zero on small Boolean-function datasets using Mat_DNF and exact accuracy, rather than the original grokking setup and time-course measures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own accuracy results for ordinary learning, noise-expansion, and over-iteration. Its discussion of grokking itself is a comparison, not a result from the cited study. Boolean-network recovery counts are not held-out accuracy results and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study learns Boolean DNFs with Mat_DNF. It invokes grokking only as an analogy for its 'over-iteration' operation. Over-iteration means a fixed number of extra updates (e.g. 20) after the first zero-error solution. The study reports end-point exact accuracy versus domain ratio. It never tracks test accuracy over training time, never shows accuracy sitting at chance after training saturates, never shows a jump to near-perfect, and never measures a delay against training-set size. The over-iteration gain is a related but different construct: a modest end-point accuracy improvement from forced extra steps. It is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that noise-expansion and over-iteration improve generalizability on scarce data by shifting which root of the cost function (learned DNF) is found. They also conclude that these operations explain the high recovery rates in their Boolean-network experiments. They mention grokking only as an analogous idea, that continuing after training saturation can help. They measure no grokking time course.
record.recipe_differences: Mat_DNF learns explicit matricized DNFs using a logically inspired cost function and Adam, on random Boolean functions and Boolean-network data; the paper measures exact accuracy over Boolean domains rather than the original study’s algorithmic-task training and test-accuracy trajectory.
record.method_sensitivity: Accuracy is reported to depend on noise-expansion and over-iteration; the tested domain ratio also varies. The paper separately varies β for its added penalty term.

fits_no_version.finding: Continuing to train a single-layer DNF network for a fixed number of extra updates after zero training error raises end-point exact accuracy at most domain ratios (Fig. 1). At dr=0.5 over-iteration also cuts the distance to the target from 7.5 to 4.2 (Table 1). No time course is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training past zero training error can select a better-generalizing zero-loss solution in small Boolean-function learners (an end-point effect, not a measured delayed jump).

record.code_released: Mat_DNF is available upon request as an octave program.
record.problems: The random-DNF experiments are small (5 variables); the implementation is described as naive and the authors note the experiment scale is small. Results are averages over 100 trials but no error bars or other uncertainty estimates are stated. The paper does not track test accuracy across optimization time or test how delay varies with training-set size.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for each point in the Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 curves: the text describes the trends across domain ratios, but does not provide the individual plotted values. Boolean-network recovery counts and formula comparisons were left out because they are not held-out accuracy results for the delayed-generalization behavior.

untested.parts: Test accuracy over optimization time; a chance-level plateau after training saturation; a sudden jump to near-perfect; delay versus training-set size. None of these is measured.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T2' and its limits_scope label for V1 are overturned. The paper provides no measurement of delayed generalization over training time; the grokking mention in Sect. 5.3 is a comparison with Power et al. The Boolean-network recovery results are irrelevant to all versions.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not track a test-accuracy jump over optimization time, show test accuracy staying at chance for a long period after training accuracy saturates, or measure whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.

rows.subject: Mat_DNF
rows.size_stated: n = 5 variables; random DNF with three disjuncts
rows.measure: Exact accuracy acc_DNF over the full domain
rows.baseline: acc_dr, the stated expected accuracy of memorizing learning data and guessing randomly on unseen data
rows.value: acc_DNF is always (and slightly) above acc_dr for all dr’s
rows.note: The paper says this is evidence of generalization beyond memorization and random guessing. It reports a sweep over domain ratios, not an optimization-time test-accuracy trajectory.
rows.check: This is ordinary learning stopped at the first zero-error root, compared with the memorize-and-guess baseline. It is a generalization level, not a delayed-generalization time course, so it does not bear on V1.

rows.subject: Mat_DNF
rows.size_stated: n = 5 variables; random DNF with three disjuncts
rows.operation_detail: Noise-expansion: append a random bit vector to each learning input
rows.measure: Exact accuracy acc_DNF_noise over the full domain
rows.value: acc_DNF_noise ≈ acc_DNF_over > acc_DNF at most dr’s
rows.note: The authors interpret noise-expansion as causing extra parameter-update steps and helping find another root of the cost function. The paper does not report a long-delay jump.
rows.check: Noise-expansion is the study's own input manipulation compared with ordinary learning. It measures neither delay nor time course, so it does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: Mat_DNF
rows.size_stated: n = 5 variables; random DNF with three disjuncts
rows.operation_detail: Over-iteration: continue learning after a zero-error root, with extra_update = 20 for the Fig. 1 curve
rows.measure: Exact accuracy acc_DNF_over over the full domain
rows.value: acc_DNF_noise ≈ acc_DNF_over > acc_DNF at most dr’s
rows.note: The stated result is an accuracy improvement from continued learning after learning error reaches zero, not a measured delayed rise from chance to near-perfect accuracy.
rows.check: Over-iteration (a fixed 20 extra updates past zero error) slightly raises end-point accuracy. No trajectory, chance-level plateau or delay is measured. This is a related construct; it is moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Mat_DNF
rows.operation_detail: Noise-expansion: append a 5-dimensional random bit vector to each interpretation vector
rows.measure: Exact accuracy acc_DNF_noise over the full domain
rows.baseline: acc_dr = 0.5 ⋅ (1 + dr), the stated memorization-and-random-guess baseline; ordinary acc_DNF is shown in Fig. 2 but its value at this ratio is not stated
rows.note: The paper states this is an average and describes it as obtained by noise-expansion. At dr = 0.1, the stated baseline formula gives 0.55; the result is above that baseline but is not near-perfect.
rows.check: 0.817 at dr=0.1 is the noise-expansion result (the paper labels it acc_DNF, but it is noise-expanded). Its baseline acc_dr is 0.55. It is the study's own method result and contains no time course.

rows.subject: Mat_DNF
rows.operation_detail: Train with the added penalty term β ⋅ Jint; no over-iteration
rows.note: This compares a penalty setting with β = 0; it measures accuracy but does not measure the post-overfitting delay or time-course named by V1.
rows.check: This compares the study's own penalty term β·Jint with β=0 (0.824 vs 0.736). It is a method comparison, not a grokking measure, and arguably should not be a row.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Mat_DNF on the tested random DNF and ϕ6 settings
reader_labels.reason: The results report generalization above the memorization-and-guessing baseline and improvement from continuing after zero learning error, but do not show the claimed delayed near-perfect test-accuracy jump or a delay that increases as the dataset shrinks (R1–R4).
